newsitem.title: USA: NASA mulls whether to send next astronaut to Mir.
newsitem.headline: NASA mulls whether to send next astronaut to Mir.

text.p: The decision whether to send a replacement U.S. astronaut to Russia's troubled Mir space station in September will rest on the assignment's likelihood of being safe and productive, a NASA official said on Sunday.

"There are two aspects to sending astronauts up to the MIR space station. First, is it safe? And secondly, is there a scientific and technical reason for doing that?" Daniel Goldin, NASA's administator, said on CNN's "Late Edition."
Navy Cmdr. Wendy Lawrence, 37, is slated to begin a four-month stay on Mir in September, replacing British-born American Michael Foale, the fifth NASA astronaut to live and work on the station.

The U.S. space agency will wait for an evaluation and recommendation from the three teams that are looking at the problems of the 11-year-old space station before deciding to launch Lawrence, Goldin said.
"... There is no commitment to send Wendy up unless we believe it's safe and productive," Goldin said, adding that just sending someone to sit on the station would not be appropriate.
"... It cannot be productive, because we have to get the Mir space station back into shape," he said. "But we will be looking at this, and we will not send Wendy up unless it's appropriate."
Mir lost half its power on June 25 after a collision with an unmanned cargo craft damaged a science module and cut off energy supplies from some solar panels.
Since then there was an unexplained malfunction in all the station's gyroscope and a mystery leak from the punctured module.

"We don't believe that it is a serious problem, but we're going to analyse it, try and understand it, and make sure that there isn't a safety problem, because safety is the most important issue on board that station," Goldin said.
